Date/Time: 2026-02-19 20:00 EST
Duration: ~41 minutes
Attendees: Noah Ellis (Redwood Marketing), Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Singh (Redwood SE), Lina Ortiz (HaloAI Head of ML Product), Samir Patel (HaloAI Growth), Derek Wu (HaloAI CTO)

---

[00:00] Noah: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the "Insights Session" — this is for the HaloAI customer spotlight. Quick reminder: we're recording, and we'll share the edit, okay?
[00:08] Lina: Yep, all good on our end.
[00:10] Maya: Thanks, Lina. I'm Maya, I'm the AE who worked with the Halo team — Ravi from our SE team also here for any technical bits.
[00:17] Ravi: hey — hi, thanks for doing this.
[00:19] Samir: Great — excited. Trying to keep it short but useful.

[00:25] Noah: Cool. Lina, can you kick off with a 60-second overview of HaloAI and what you're using Redwood for day-to-day?
[00:33] Lina: Sure. So HaloAI makes real-time product recommendations for retail publishers, um, we run a mix of retrieval plus a light generative layer for descriptions and personalization. We started with hosted endpoints — other providers — that was fine for prototyping, but when we moved to high QPS and sub-100ms targets it got pricey and brittle. We onboarded Redwood last year to handle inference at scale, and we use a mix of Redwood Hosted for background batch jobs and Redwood Dedicated pools for our real-time endpoints.
[01:05] Maya: Nice. Was cost the main driver or reliability?
[01:08] Lina: Both. Cost per token went down about 35% after we adopted Redwood Optimize suggestions, and p50 latency dropped from roughly 120ms to about 60ms on our main recommendation route. But equally important was predictable tail latency and the ability to do canary rollouts when model changes occur.
[01:28] Samir: The marketing team loves that latency improvement — our CTR lifted too, probably because the product felt snappier.

[01:36] Noah: That's a great nugget. Quick aside: can you name a specific launch where Redwood participation mattered?
[01:41] Lina: Yeah, our November collection push — we launched an A/B where variant A used the previous hosted flow, variant B used Redwood Dedicated with prefix caching and KV caching. Variant B showed a 4.2% lift in conversions on the product detail page. That was big for the business case.
[01:58] Derek: To add, from infra side, Redwood's routing and autoscale saved us from over-provisioning GPUs. We set a predictable reserved cap and burst to cloud when needed. That lowered our monthly committed spend while keeping the SLAs we needed.

[02:15] Ravi: quick technical note — we recommended model quantization to int8 and lower batch sizes for tail-sensitive routes. That was something you accepted in the second month, Lina?
[02:24] Lina: Correct. We also tried a lighter model family for small prompt lengths which cut cost and had negligible quality impact.

[02:31] Noah: nice. For listeners, can you give a short description of the integration work — timeline, teams involved, what was the rough lift?
[02:38] Lina: Integration was about three sprints. The Red- — Redwood SE team helped with model packaging, we did VPC peering for the private endpoints, and our infra team handled service mesh routing. There were a few gotchas — the first week of prefix cache tuning required iteration. Overall, low friction.
[02:56] Maya: can you describe the security side — any enterprise controls required?
[03:00] Derek: We needed SOC 2 evidence, demo of audit logs, and KMS integration. There was a little confusion early on — "sock two" in the notes — but the Redwood security pack covered everything. KMS set up took a day, and we turned on audit logging.
[03:15] Ravi: also note, we validated that the PV C — the VPC peering and private control plane worked in our staging.

[03:24] Noah: transcriptions sometimes mess up acronyms. Back to marketing — Samir, what did you pull for promotional material?
[03:29] Samir: We pulled a quote from Lina about the 4.2% lift and a short tech snippet about sub-100ms latency. We also have a screenshot of the Redwood Console dashboard showing token-level costs that we might use in the case study.
[03:42] Noah: Perfect — we'll need a signed quote. Lina, are you comfortable with that?
[03:46] Lina: Yeah, as long as we can review the final phrasing.

[03:50] Noah: Totally. We'll send the copy for approval.

[03:54] -- Technical aside segment --
[03:55] Ravi: one quick deep dive for the tech audience: the biggest win was prefix/KV cache on our high-frequency keys. We cached user preferences and session prefixes which meant small prompts didn't need full autoregression every time. Also, for large recommendation candidates we used Redwood batching and batching that preserves latency SLOs.
[04:19] Derek: we had to pay attention to KV eviction policies and cache warming on rollouts, otherwise first-hit latency spikes were noticeable.
[04:29] Lina: we created synthetic pre-warm traffic during canaries and it smoothed things out.

[04:36] Noah: Were there any surprises in the onboarding?
[04:39] Lina: A couple. First, we underestimated the amount of prompt engineering needed to maintain tone across locales. Second, our initial quantization run had a small downgrade on rare tokens which we addressed by pinning a small submodule to float16.
[04:55] Maya: good call on targeted float16. I'm noting that — shows the value of hybrid quantization.

[05:02] Noah: For the case study narrative, what's the one thing you'd want customers to take away? Lina?
[05:06] Lina: I'd say: Production inference is more than raw model size. It's routing, caching, and operational controls. Redwood let us treat inference like a product — reproducible rollouts, measurable cost, and predictable latency.
[05:22] Samir: From marketing: "faster, cheaper, and more reliable" — that's a nice tagline, if you want one-liners.

[05:28] -- Interruption, small cross-talk --
[05:30] (brief noise)

[05:33] Noah: great. Let's surface some metrics for the one-pager. Maya, can you read back the numbers we have?
[05:37] Maya: Sure: p50 latency down from ~120ms to ~60ms. Token cost improvement about 35% after Optimize and quantization. Conversion lift on the product page A/B was +4.2%. Cost predictability improved — our committed monthly GPU spend dropped 18% through reserved + burst policy.
[05:54] Derek: those are good. Also mention the rollouts — we did canary -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over two days for model swaps.

[06:04] Noah: listeners will like the timeline — three sprints to integrate, saw results in one month for cost/latency.

[06:11] -- Editing note: skip to audience Q&A (we had an internal Q from product marketing) --
[06:13] Q (PM): Did you need a dedicated compliance review for EU data residency?
[06:17] Lina: Yes — for EU customers we enabled Private deployment in-region and used customer-managed keys. The Redwood team provided region-specific guidance and template configs. Took about two weeks to certify.

[06:29] Q (PM): How do you measure model quality drift?
[06:32] Lina: We tied evaluations to a small set of prompts and tracked changes in predicted CTR + manual review. Redwood Optimize's regression alerts flagged two small regressions last quarter; we rolled back and iterated.

[06:45] Noah: Nice — practical example.

[06:47] -- Middle of recording: candid discussion about org alignment --
[06:48] Samir: There's some internal pushback: product wants the nicest outputs, infra wants the cheapest path. Redwood's tuning controls gave us the option to set cost-quality profiles per route which helped mediate that.
[07:04] Maya: That's a common pattern. You can have route-level configs for quantization, cache TTLs, and fallbacks.

[07:12] Derek: We used automatic fallback policy when Dedicated capacity was saturated — fallback to hosted lower-cost model for non-critical requests. That kept user-facing errors near zero.

[07:24] Noah: sounds like a good engineering compromise.

[07:27] -- Nearing the end: marketing use-cases and quotes --
[07:28] Samir: for the case study, I'm asking for one sentence about business impact and one sentence about experience working with Redwood. Lina?
[07:35] Lina: Business impact: "Redwood allowed HaloAI to cut inference cost and improve response latency, delivering a measurable uplift in product conversions." Experience: "Working with Redwood's AE and SE teams made the migration fast and low-friction."
[07:53] Noah: fantastic. We'll send that as a suggested quote for approval.

[07:57] -- Closing logistics and approvals --
[07:58] Maya: Our next steps: 1) Marketing will edit the recording and send a clip; 2) we'll draft the one-pager; 3) Ravi will attach technical graphs. Deadline for Halo review is Mar 3.
[08:13] Lina: Sounds good. Also please blur any internal KPI numbers in the public doc unless we sign off.
[08:19] Noah: Understood.

[08:21] -- Wrap and sign-off --
[08:22] Noah: Anything else? Derek: nope. Samir: nothing.
[08:25] Lina: good to go.
[08:27] Maya: Thanks everyone — appreciate you taking the time.
[08:30] Noah: End recording.
